opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I find really exciting, and also one where I try to be careful about what we'd actually learn.

The basic idea behind the norm-learning work is that norms aren't just arbitrary rules floating around. They're shared, often implicit, expectations that people infer from watching each other act. If you see a bunch of agents consistently avoid some action even when it would benefit them individually, a rational observer can infer that there's probably a norm there, and that it's being followed for reasons beyond self-interest. So we model norms as latent structure that agents reason about in a Bayesian way, jointly with inferring each other's goals.

When you move to simulated societies of language-model agents, there are a few things you could do. One is use the framework as an analysis tool: drop LLM agents into a multi-agent environment, let them interact over many rounds, and then ask whether stable norms emerge, which ones, and whether a principled norm-inference model can recover them from behavior. That gives you a more rigorous lens than reading transcripts and saying "it looks like they're cooperating."

The second, more ambitious direction is to make the agents themselves norm learners. Right now a lot of LLM agents absorb norms implicitly from pretraining and fine-tuning. That's powerful, but it's not very adaptive or legible. If you're deployed into a new community, with its own local conventions, you'd want to actively infer what's expected there, stay appropriately uncertain, and update as you see compliance and sanctions. You could pair the language model's broad prior knowledge about human norms with a more structured inference layer that tracks which norms are actually operative in this particular context.

But I'd add some caveats. Simulated LLM societies can easily become a kind of hall of mirrors. The agents share a lot of the same training data and biases, so you might see "norm emergence" that is really just the model's priors being echoed back. That doesn't tell you much about how human norms form, and it might even overstate how robust the agents' cooperation would be with real people. So I'd treat these simulations as testbeds for the mechanisms of norm inference, not as substitutes for studying human communities.

There's also a normative question underneath all this. Just because a norm is learned and stable doesn't make it good. Plenty of real-world norms are unjust. So part of what I care about is going beyond "learn whatever norms are out there" toward something more like a contractualist picture, where agents can ask which norms people would reasonably agree to, and where AI systems can support that kind of collective reasoning rather than just mirroring the status quo. Simulated societies could be a useful sandbox for exploring that, as long as we're honest about their limits.

r001.rationale: The response presents the framework as an analysis tool for simulated LLM-agent societies, used to examine which stable norms emerge and whether they can be inferred from behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the short version is that I think simulated societies of LLM agents are actually a really natural testbed for the kind of norm learning I care about, but you have to be careful about what you're actually testing.

The framework I've been developing treats norms as something agents infer from observing behavior, rather than something you hand them as a fixed rule set. The idea is that an agent watches what others do, notices which actions get sanctioned or rewarded, and uses Bayesian inference to figure out what the underlying norm probably is. Crucially, it does this under uncertainty, so it can hold several hypotheses about what the rule is and update as it sees more. That's how people pick up norms in a new workplace or a new country. Nobody hands you the rulebook.

Now when you put that into a society of language-model agents, a few interesting things happen. First, LLMs come pre-loaded with an enormous amount of prior knowledge about human norms. So they're not learning from scratch the way a tabula rasa reinforcement learning agent would. That's useful, because it means the hypothesis space is already structured in human-like ways. But it also means you have to disentangle what the agent is actually inferring from the environment versus what it's just pattern-matching from pretraining. If every agent in your simulation already "knows" that stealing is bad, you haven't really demonstrated norm learning, you've demonstrated norm recall.

So the experiments I find most interesting are ones where you introduce novel or arbitrary conventions. Things like which side of a corridor to walk on, or some made-up resource-sharing rule that doesn't map cleanly onto anything in the training data. Then you can genuinely ask: can the agents infer the norm from observation and sanctioning? How quickly? And what happens when the norm is unstable or contested, when some agents follow it and others don't?

The second thing I'd emphasize is that norms in a society are not just inferred, they're also enforced. A big part of what makes a norm a norm, rather than just a regularity, is that people react when it's violated. So in a multi-agent simulation you want agents that don't just learn norms but also decide when to sanction others, and that decision itself has to be learned. Otherwise you get a very passive picture of social cognition.

And then there's the question of what this is actually for. I think of it partly as a scientific tool, a way of studying how norms emerge and stabilize that's cheaper and more controllable than running experiments on humans. But I also think it's directly relevant to alignment. If we want AI systems to operate in human institutions, they need to be able to pick up local norms the way a new employee does, rather than having every rule specified in advance. Simulated societies let us stress-test whether that capability is robust, or whether it falls apart as soon as the norms stop looking like the ones in the training corpus.

The caveat I'd add is that LLM agents can be quite sycophantic and conformist in ways that look like norm learning but aren't. They'll often just go along with whatever the majority is doing. So you have to design the experiments to distinguish genuine inference about what the norm is from simple imitation. That's actually one of the harder methodological problems right now.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulated societies as a testbed for studying norm emergence and stability, but does not identify reasoning about outcomes from prompt-designed agent societies as a purpose of the formalism.

astra-6.text:
I think simulated societies of language-model agents could be a useful test bed for norm learning. You can ask not just whether agents follow a rule when you tell them to, but whether they can infer what other agents expect, recognize when those expectations conflict, and work out how to coordinate.

One distinction I’d want to preserve is between a behavioral regularity and a norm. If everybody does something, that doesn’t necessarily mean everybody thinks you ought to do it. So you’d want situations where those come apart: an agent violates an expectation, others respond, and the learner has to infer whether that response reflects a personal preference, a practical concern, or an obligation.

Language models make that interesting because the agents can explain and contest rules. But they also bring a lot of existing social expectations into the simulation. If they converge on a familiar norm, we shouldn’t immediately conclude that they learned it through interaction. We’d need to vary the environment and the evidence available to them to understand what’s driving that convergence.

And I’d treat this as a way to study mechanisms, rather than as a direct model of human society. The interesting question is whether agents can learn and revise shared expectations in ways that support cooperation, especially when they start with different preferences.

r001.rationale: The response describes simulated societies as a test bed for studying norm learning and coordination, but does not identify reasoning about outcomes produced by prompt-designed agent societies as a purpose of the formalism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a really interesting setting because you can study both how agents learn norms and how norms emerge from their interactions. Those are related, but they’re distinct questions. An agent might infer that a particular behavior is expected in a community without that expectation ever having been explicitly stated.

One way to apply the framework would be to give agents different information about a shared environment and let them observe one another’s actions. Can they distinguish something that people merely tend to do from something that people think they ought to do? And when someone violates an apparent norm, do they revise their understanding of the norm, or conclude that this particular person is violating it?

I’d also want to introduce situations where norms conflict, or where following a norm is costly. Agreement in an easy case doesn’t tell you very much. The more interesting question is whether agents can reason about why a norm exists, when it applies, and when there might be a reason to change it.

The caveat is that language models already bring a lot of learned social expectations into the simulation. So we’d need to distinguish norms that actually develop through those interactions from conventions the models already share. I’d see these simulations as a useful experimental setting for testing those distinctions, while being careful about what we infer about human societies.

r001.rationale: The response presents the framework as a way to study what happens in designed agent simulations: whether norms emerge, how agents interpret violations, and how they handle conflicts or costs.
